content: The final data analysis after the data lock was not blinded to the treatment groups, and no interim analysis was planned for the trial. However, no adverse reactions to the study milk were reported, and the blinding procedure was maintained until the end of the study. The risk of contamination (performance bias) was unclear, as it was not explicitly addressed. The study received ethical approval from the Health and Disability Ethics Committee of the Ministry of Health, New Zealand (14/NTB/152). It was registered in the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ACTRN12614000918628). There were no other clear signs of bias. Recruitment bias, baseline imbalance, loss of clusters, incorrect analysis, and compatibility with individual RCTs were not applicable as these domains were only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. In the Maldonado 2007 study, a double-blind RCT with two arms was conducted. Participants were healthy young children aged 12–30 months from Granada, Spain, with no relevant pathology from birth until inclusion in the trial. All participants had a varied diet appropriate for their age, including cow milk. Children were randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group 1 (n=16) received 500 mL of iron-fortified follow-on formula, and Group 2 (n=17) received 500 mL of cow milk. The intervention lasted four months, and the milk was provided in identical packages to maintain blinding. Outcomes measured included weight, length, BMI, hemoglobin, serum ferritin, serum iron, serum transferrin, mean corpuscular volume, hematocrit, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin. All children had been breastfed for 6–8 months and received follow-on formula until their first year of life. The iron content in the fortified formula was 2 mg/100 mL. The study used a computer random number generator for random sequence generation, ensuring low risk of selection bias. Allocation concealment was achieved as participants and investigators enrolling participants could not foresee assignments; only personnel providing the milk packages knew the assignments. Baseline outcome measurements showed no significant differences between groups, indicating low risk of confounding. However, baseline characteristics were not reported, leading to a high risk of selection bias. All participants completed the study, and results were shown, indicating low risk of attrition bias. Milk was provided in identical packages to maintain double blinding, and only personnel providing the milk knew group assignments, ensuring low risk of performance bias. Blinding of outcome assessment was not reported, leading to unclear risk of detection bias. Contamination risk was unclear. The research protocol was approved by the Ethical Committee of the University of Granada, Spain, and there were no other clear signs of bias. In the Morley 1999 study, a randomized controlled trial with three arms was conducted. Participants were healthy 9-month-old infants from three centers in the UK (Leicester, Norwich, and Nottingham). Infants were born after 36 or more completed weeks of gestation, weighed >2500 g, and were either singletons or sole survivors from multiple pregnancies. Children (n=493) were assigned to one of three groups: Group 1 received formula with 0.5 mg iron/L, Group 2 received formula with 9 mg iron/L, and Group 3 received formula with 2 mg iron/L as ferrous sulfate. Formula milk was supplied in powdered form, with tins labeled as “formula 28” for iron-fortified formula and “formula 61” for unfortified formula. The code was not revealed until the study was completed, and all data had been entered and checked. Milk was supplied ad libitum to participants’ homes, and parents were given written and verbal instructions on milk preparation. For this review, only groups 1 and 3 were analyzed. Outcomes measured included mental and psychomotor development, growth, and hematological indices. The study was funded by Wyeth Laboratories. Randomization schedules were prepared by an independent statistician using permuted blocks of random length, ensuring low risk of selection bias. Allocation concealment was achieved using consecutively numbered opaque sealed envelopes, ensuring low risk of selection bias. Groups were well balanced in terms of pre-randomization anthropometry and developmental status, indicating low risk of confounding. Demographic characteristics and pre-randomization measures were similar between groups, ensuring low risk of selection bias. Missing data were similar between groups, and participant flow throughout the study was provided, indicating low risk of attrition bias. Formula milk was supplied in coded tins, and the code was not revealed until the study was completed, ensuring low risk of performance bias. Staff at the three follow-up centers were blinded to dietary allocation. The code was not revealed until the study was completed, ensuring low risk of detection bias. There were no other clear signs of bias. In the Rivera 2010 study, a double-blind cluster RCT with two arms was conducted. Participants were children aged 12–30 months who were beneficiaries of a program distributing whole milk at subsidized prices in Mexico. Twelve milk distribution clusters were randomized to receive either non-fortified milk or fortified milk. A total of 567 participants were enrolled, with Group 1 (n=210) receiving non-fortified milk and Group 2 (n=357) receiving fortified milk. The fortified milk group was larger per program officials’ request to provide fortified milk to as many children as possible. The fortified milk contained 1 mcg folic acid, 8 mg vitamin C, and 24 mcg folic acid, with other nutrient content being similar. The protocol was reviewed and approved by the Human Subjects and Ethics Committee of the National Public Health Institute, Mexico. Authors reported adjusting for cluster effects. Outcomes measured included anemia (based on hemoglobin) and iron deficiency (based on serum ferritin and serum soluble transferrin) improvement from baseline classifications of mild anemia, moderate anemia, or mild-to-moderate anemia. Monthly average daily milk intake during the intervention was also measured. Random sequence generation was reported as randomized, but the method was not described, leading to unclear risk of selection bias. Allocation concealment was not reported, leading to unclear risk of selection bias. Baseline concentrations of hemoglobin, serum transferrin, prevalence of anemia and iron deficiency, anthropometric scores, and socioeconomic index were similar between groups, indicating low risk of confounding. However, differences were found between children included and not included in the final models for serum transferrin and serum ferritin, particularly in the fortified milk group. Of the 767 participants, 635 (17% attrition) completed the first follow-up at six months, and 584 (24% attrition) completed the second follow-up. Reasons for attrition included refusal to participate and dropouts without measurements, indicating low risk of attrition bias. The study was reported as double-blinded, with randomization blinded to researchers, personnel in milk distribution centers, and technical staff until the end of the trial. The color code of milk packages was unknown to researchers, field workers, and program beneficiaries, ensuring low risk of performance bias. The study was unblinded only after data analysis, ensuring low risk of detection bias. Contamination was unlikely as all milk distributed in each center was either fortified or unfortified, ensuring low risk of performance bias. All outcomes stated in the methods section were reported, ensuring low risk of reporting bias. There were no other clear signs of bias. However, recruitment bias was high as children were recruited after clusters were randomized. Baseline imbalance was unclear. No clusters were lost to follow-up, and regression and logistic models adjusting for cluster effects were used for comparisons, ensuring low risk of incorrect analysis. The cluster design did not seem to affect the findings, ensuring low risk of compatibility issues with individual RCTs. In the Sazawal 2007 study, a double-blind, community-based RCT with four arms was conducted. Participants were children aged 1–3 years from a peri-urban population in New Delhi, India. All families with children aged 1–3 years were invited to participate. The four arms were divided into two trials. Two arms evaluated the efficacy of a milk preparation fortified with probiotics compared to a preparation without fortification in a non-factorial design with joint randomization. In the other two-armed trial, children (n=633) were randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group 1 (n=316) received fortified milk, and Group 2 (n=317) received control milk. Groups 1 and 2 were implemented concurrently with another two-armed trial with Groups 3 and 4. For this review, only children from Groups 1, 2, and 3 were used. Children with severe anemia at baseline received a therapeutic dose of iron for three months in addition to their milk supplement. Supplementation continued for one year.
